theme: Difficult times; preach the word; finish the race
readingInstruction: Read 2 Timothy 3:1-4:22. These are Paul’s last recorded words. Notice the warning about hard times, the great statement about Scripture, the solemn charge to preach, and Paul’s own testimony as he faces death.
settingTheScene: Paul writes his final instructions to Timothy. He knows his time is short. The church will face difficult days, and false teachers will multiply. His solution is not new methods but the faithful preaching of the word. These verses contain the most important statement in the Bible about the nature of Scripture, and they also give a deeply moving portrait of a servant at the end of his race.
observation: “But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty” (3:1).
“Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (3:12).
“And how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (3:15).
“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (3:16).
“Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching” (4:2).
“For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions” (4:3).
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7).
“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed” (4:17).
interpretation:
Paul says that “in the last days there will come times of difficulty.” The last days began with Christ’s first coming, so this is a description of the whole era. People will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, abusive, disobedient, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, haters of good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, “having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power.” Timothy is to avoid such people. Paul contrasts them with Timothy: “You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings.” Then a sober truth: “Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.”

Timothy must continue in what he has learned. He knows from whom he learned it and has known “the sacred writings” from childhood, “which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Then the great statement: “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.” The word “breathed out” (theopneustos) means that Scripture originates in God. It is his word, just as a human’s breath carries his words. It is profitable in four ways: it teaches what is true, reproves what is wrong, corrects the path, and trains in righteousness. And its goal is that we be complete, equipped for every good work. Scripture is sufficient for the life of faith.

Chapter 4 begins with a solemn charge, “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead.” The command is simple: “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.” The reason is that people will turn away. “They will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.” Timothy is to be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill his ministry.

Then Paul looks at his own end: “For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.” The letter closes with personal notes: Demas has deserted him, only Luke is with him, and he asks for Mark, his cloak, and his books and parchments. At his first defense, no one came to stand by him, “but the Lord stood by me and strengthened me.” “The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”
connection: Matthew 24:9-13 and 2 Peter 3:3 also warn of hard times. John 15:20 promises persecution. 2 Peter 1:20-21 explains the origin of Scripture. Psalm 19:7-11 and 119:105 praise Scripture’s value. Luke 24:44-47 shows Scripture pointing to Christ. Acts 20:24 is Paul’s earlier statement about finishing his course. Philippians 2:17 and 1:21-23 also use the drink offering image. 1 Peter 5:4 promises a crown to faithful shepherds. Acts 23:11 and 27:23-24 recall times Christ stood by Paul. Hebrews 4:12 speaks of the living word.
application:
Choose a time and place for reading the Bible every day, and commit to it. Ask God to use Scripture to teach, reprove, correct, and train you.

Let 3:16-17 stay with you.

Ask whether you are finishing well. What is one thing you need to do to keep the faith?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that all Scripture is breathed out by him.
Ask him to use it to teach, reprove, correct, and train you.
Ask him to help you finish well.
